notes: \cpara{Pooh-Bah's line in \textsc{The Mikado}, said of the made-up details of an execution that never took place. Tversky and Kahneman quote the same line in the 1983 paper the post cites (p.~308).}
\cpara{Defines the conjunction fallacy and gives the Reagan example. The rule stated, that a conjunction is never likelier than either part, is correct.}
\cpara{Gives the explanation: people judge by representativeness, and an added detail can make an outcome seem more typical, so the two claims ``average out''.}
\cpara{States the moral. It is Tversky and Kahneman's own conclusion about scenarios, in the paper the post cites: added details ``can only lower probability'' (1983, p.~308).}
\cpara{Names, ``hypothetically speaking'', where the fallacy should show up: futurists' detailed histories and bundles of unsupported claims.}
\cpara{Says that correcting yourself on a direct comparison is a patch for one problem, not a general fix.}
\cpara{Recalls the 1982 experiment with professional forecasters, in which each group saw only one statement, and asks what they could have done.}
\cpara{Repeats, in new words, the point made two paragraphs earlier (``slapping a band-aid on the problem, not fixing it in general'').}
\cpara{Answers, with ``It seems to me'': the forecasters would need to notice the word ``and'', recoil from it, and cut their estimate by a factor of four or more.}

\cpara{Adds a second remedy, for the other group: think of the many reasons the plain event could happen. With this the post covers both sides of the comparison, since the group that saw no ``and'' could have raised its estimate.}
\cpara{Applies the remedy to the Reagan subjects: add the improbabilities, measured in bits, instead of averaging them.}

\clogic{Loosely stated. Adding the two numbers gives the absurdity of both claims only if they are independent. In general $P(A \mbox{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B \mid A)$, so the second term must be the absurdity of B given A. In a causal story, where one detail makes the next likelier, adding the details' separate absurdities overstates the penalty.}

\cpara{Turns to the dice experiment, where 65 percent chose a sequence dominated by a shorter one it contains. It sets aside noticing the inclusion as a patch, and exact calculation as not always possible.}
\cpara{Contrasts the losing thought (``highest proportion of green to red'') with the winning one (``Sequence 1 is short!'').}

\clogic{Shortness decides this case only because sequence 2 contains sequence 1. Between sequences that do not contain each other it can mislead. With this die, GGGGGG has probability $(2/3)^6 \approx 0.088$ at a given position and RRRRR has $(1/3)^5 \approx 0.0041$: the longer one is about 21 times likelier.}
\cpara{States the general remedy, the post's answer to its own question: feel every added detail as a burden. No evidence is given that people who feel details this way make fewer errors.}
\cpara{An anecdote: the author persuades a listener by comparing ``universes replicate for any reason'' with a longer chain of claims.}
\cpara{Draws the lesson: support for one claim in a package is not support for the package.}
\cpara{Tells the reader to ask of each detail ``How do we know this detail?'', with a hypothetical futurist scenario about China as the example.}
\cpara{Quotes, as scripture, two sentences from the author's own ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' (2006), from the seventh virtue, simplicity. The post does not say whose words they are.}
